front:
Shared responsibility model

Who secures what, in the cloud?
back: AWS secures the cloud itself: hardware, software, networking and facilities. The customer secures what they put in the cloud: data, identities, configuration, guest OS.

src.title: AWS: Shared Responsibility Model
src.q: AWS is responsible for protecting the infrastructure that runs all of the services offered in the AWS Cloud

front:
IAM

What does it control?
back: A web service for securely controlling access to AWS resources: who is authenticated and what they are authorized to do.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is IAM?
src.q: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is a web service that helps you securely control access to AWS resources

front:
IAM role

How does it differ from an IAM user?
back: An identity with permission policies that anyone who needs it can assume, instead of being tied to one person. Prefer roles for workloads and cross-account access.

src.title: AWS Docs: IAM roles
src.q: instead of being uniquely associated with one person, a role is intended to be assumable by anyone who needs it

front:
IAM role credentials

What kind of credentials does a role use?
back: No long-term password or access keys. It hands out temporary credentials, which is safer than embedding keys in code.

src.title: AWS Docs: IAM roles
src.q: a role does not have standard long-term credentials such as a password or access keys associated with it

front:
STS temporary credentials

How long can they last?
back: From a few minutes to several hours. After expiry AWS no longer accepts them. Used for role switching, federation and cross-account access.

src.title: AWS Docs: Temporary security credentials
src.q: They can be configured to last for anywhere from a few minutes to several hours

front:
MFA on the root user

Which accounts should have it?
back: The root user of every account (standalone, management and member) and IAM users. Prefer phishing-resistant MFA like passkeys or security keys.

src.title: AWS Docs: MFA in IAM
src.q: You can enable MFA for the AWS account root user of all AWS accounts

front:
IAM policy evaluation

What happens first when a request arrives?
back: AWS authenticates the principal, then evaluates policies. An explicit deny always wins, then an allow is needed, otherwise the request is implicitly denied.

src.title: AWS Docs: Policy evaluation logic
src.q: AWS first authenticates the principal that makes the request, if necessary

front:
Service control policies (SCPs)

Do they grant permissions?
back: No. SCPs set the maximum available permissions for IAM users and roles in an organization's accounts. Identity or resource policies still must allow the action.

src.title: AWS Docs: Service control policies
src.q: SCPs offer central control over the maximum available permissions for the IAM users and IAM roles in your organization

front:
AWS Control Tower

What does it set up?
back: A multi-account environment following prescriptive best practices, with guardrails and governance across accounts.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is AWS Control Tower?
src.q: AWS Control Tower offers a straightforward way to set up and govern an AWS multi-account environment

front:
IAM Identity Center

Who is it for?
back: Connects workforce users to AWS accounts and managed applications with single sign-on, often federated with an existing directory.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is IAM Identity Center?
src.q: AWS IAM Identity Center is the AWS solution for connecting your workforce users to AWS managed applications

front:
Security group

What does it control, and is it stateful?
back: Inbound and outbound traffic for the resources it is attached to (like an EC2 instance). Allow rules only, and it is stateful, so return traffic is automatic.

src.title: AWS Docs: Security groups
src.q: it controls the inbound and outbound traffic for the instance

front:
Network ACL

Where does it apply, and how does it differ from a security group?
back: A subnet-level firewall with its own rules, similar to security group rules. Stateless, with numbered allow and deny rules.

src.title: AWS Docs: Network ACLs
src.q: You can use the default network ACL for your VPC, or you can create a custom network ACL for your VPC with rules similar to your security group rules

front:
NAT gateway

What does it let private subnets do?
back: Lets instances in a private subnet reach services outside the VPC, while external services cannot start connections to them.

src.title: AWS Docs: NAT gateways
src.q: You can use a NAT gateway so that instances in a private subnet can connect to services outside your VPC

front:
AWS PrivateLink

What problem does it solve?
back: Privately connects your VPC to services as if they were in your VPC, without going over the public internet.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is AWS PrivateLink?
src.q: AWS PrivateLink is a highly available, scalable technology that you can use to privately connect your VPC to services and resources as if they were in your VPC

front:
AWS WAF

What does it inspect?
back: HTTP(S) requests forwarded to protected resources such as CloudFront and load balancers. Use it for SQL injection and XSS rules.

src.title: AWS Docs: AWS WAF
src.q: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that lets you monitor the HTTP(S) requests that are forwarded to your protected web application resources

front:
AWS Shield

Which attacks does it address?
back: DDoS attacks at network and transport layers (3 and 4) and the application layer (7). Standard is automatic, Advanced adds more protection and support.

src.title: AWS Docs: How AWS Shield works
src.q: AWS Shield Standard and AWS Shield Advanced provide protections against Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks

front:
Amazon GuardDuty

What does it do?
back: Threat detection that continuously monitors and analyzes AWS data sources and logs in your account.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is GuardDuty?
src.q: Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors, analyzes, and processes AWS data sources and logs in your AWS environment

front:
Amazon Macie

What does it find?
back: Sensitive data, such as PII in S3, by using machine learning and pattern matching.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Macie?
src.q: Amazon Macie is a data security service that discovers sensitive data by using machine learning and pattern matching

front:
Amazon Cognito

When would you use it?
back: Sign-up, sign-in and access control for web and mobile app users: a user directory and authentication service for your customers.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Amazon Cognito?
src.q: Amazon Cognito is an identity platform for web and mobile apps

front:
AWS Secrets Manager

What does it manage?
back: Database credentials, API keys and other secrets, with retrieval and automatic rotation, so they are not hard-coded.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is AWS Secrets Manager?
src.q: AWS Secrets Manager helps you manage, retrieve, and rotate database credentials, application credentials, OAuth tokens, API keys, and other secrets throughout their lifecycles

front:
AWS Direct Connect

What does it link?
back: Your internal network to a Direct Connect location over Ethernet fiber: a private dedicated connection, not over the internet.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Direct Connect?
src.q: Direct Connect links your internal network to a Direct Connect location over a standard Ethernet fiber-optic cable

front:
AWS KMS

What does it manage?
back: Creates and controls the keys used to encrypt and sign data. Keys are protected in FIPS-validated hardware security modules. Use key policies to control access.

src.title: AWS Docs: AWS KMS overview
src.q: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) is an AWS managed service that makes it easy for you to create and control the keys used to encrypt and sign your data

front:
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)

What does it handle?
back: Creating, storing and renewing public and private SSL/TLS certificates for AWS websites and apps. Gives encryption in transit with automatic renewal.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is ACM?
src.q: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) handles the complexity of creating, storing, and renewing public and private SSL/TLS X.509 certificates and keys

front:
AWS Config

What does it record?
back: A detailed view of resource configurations, relationships, and how they changed over time. Useful for compliance checks.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is AWS Config?
src.q: AWS Config provides a detailed view of the configuration of AWS resources in your AWS account

front:
S3 Block Public Access

What does it override?
back: Bucket policies, access point policies and object permissions that would allow public access. Turn it on to prevent accidental exposure.

src.title: AWS Docs: S3 Block Public Access
src.q: S3 Block Public Access settings override these policies and permissions so that you can limit public access to these resources

front:
S3 Versioning

What can you recover from?
back: Unintended user actions and application failures: every version of every object is preserved and restorable.

src.title: AWS Docs: S3 Versioning
src.q: You can use the S3 Versioning feature to preserve, retrieve, and restore every version of every object stored in your buckets

front:
AWS Backup

What does it centralize?
back: Backup policies and monitoring across AWS services and on premises, in one place.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is AWS Backup?
src.q: AWS Backup is a fully-managed service that makes it easy to centralize and automate data protection across AWS services

front:
Elastic Load Balancing

What does it do?
back: Distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets (instances, containers, IPs) in one or more Availability Zones.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Elastic Load Balancing?
src.q: Elastic Load Balancing automatically distributes your incoming traffic across multiple targets

front:
EC2 Auto Scaling

What does it keep correct?
back: The number of EC2 instances available for the current load: adds instances on demand and removes them when not needed.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is EC2 Auto Scaling?
src.q: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling helps you ensure that you have the correct number of Amazon EC2 instances available to handle the load for your application

front:
Amazon SQS

What does a queue give you?
back: Decoupling: a durable queue between components so a producer and consumer scale and fail independently.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Amazon SQS?
src.q: offers a secure, durable, and available hosted queue that lets you integrate and decouple distributed software systems and components

front:
Amazon SNS

How does it deliver messages?
back: Publish/subscribe: publishers send to a topic and the service fans out to many subscribers.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Amazon SNS?
src.q: is a fully managed service that provides message delivery from publishers (producers) to subscribers (consumers)

front:
Amazon EventBridge

What connects components?
back: Events. A serverless event bus for building event-driven applications with routing rules.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is EventBridge?
src.q: is a serverless service that uses events to connect application components together

front:
AWS Lambda

What do you not manage?
back: Servers. Lambda runs your code and handles infrastructure, capacity provisioning, scaling and patching.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is AWS Lambda?
src.q: With Lambda, you can run code without provisioning or managing servers

front:
Amazon API Gateway

What does it publish?
back: REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs at any scale, with monitoring and security. A common front door for Lambda.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is API Gateway?
src.q: Amazon API Gateway is an AWS service for creating, publishing, maintaining, monitoring, and securing REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs at any scale

front:
AWS Fargate

What do you stop managing?
back: Clusters of virtual machines for containers: no choosing server types or scaling clusters. Serverless compute for ECS and EKS.

src.title: AWS Docs: AWS Fargate
src.q: With AWS Fargate, you no longer have to provision, configure, or scale clusters of virtual machines to run containers

front:
Route 53 failover routing

What topology does it support?
back: Active-passive failover: traffic goes to the primary until health checks fail, then to the secondary.

src.title: AWS Docs: Choosing a routing policy
src.q: Use when you want to configure active-passive failover

front:
Route 53 geolocation routing

When do you use it?
back: When you want to route traffic by the location of your users, for example for localization or compliance.

src.title: AWS Docs: Choosing a routing policy
src.q: Use when you want to route traffic based on the location of your users

front:
RDS Multi-AZ

Is the standby readable?
back: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, no. The standby is for failover support only. Use read replicas for read scaling.

src.title: AWS Docs: Multi-AZ DB instance deployments
src.q: A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment has one standby DB instance that provides failover support

front:
RDS read replica

What is it for?
back: A read-only copy of a DB instance used to offload read traffic and scale reads, not a high availability mechanism by itself.

src.title: AWS Docs: RDS read replicas
src.q: A read replica is a read-only copy of a DB instance

front:
Amazon Aurora

What engines is it compatible with?
back: A fully managed relational database engine compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL, with built-in replication across Availability Zones.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Aurora?
src.q: Amazon Aurora (Aurora) is a fully managed relational database engine

front:
DynamoDB global tables

What do they replicate across?
back: Regions (and optionally accounts), automatically. Gives multi-Region deployment with low or zero RPO.

src.title: AWS Docs: DynamoDB global tables
src.q: Global tables automatically replicate your DynamoDB table data across AWS Regions

front:
S3 replication

Where can objects be copied?
back: To one or many destination buckets, in the same or other Regions, same or different accounts.

src.title: AWS Docs: Replicating objects in S3
src.q: You can replicate objects to a single destination bucket or to multiple destination buckets

front:
DR: Backup and restore

What does it protect against?
back: Data loss or corruption. Cheapest, slowest recovery. Can cover a regional disaster if backups are replicated to another Region.

src.title: AWS Docs: Disaster recovery options in the cloud
src.q: Backup and restore is a suitable approach for mitigating against data loss or corruption

front:
DR: Pilot light

What is always on?
back: Data replication and core infrastructure like databases. The rest of the application is provisioned at recovery time.

src.title: AWS Docs: Disaster recovery options in the cloud
src.q: With the pilot light approach, you replicate your data from one Region to another and provision a copy of your core workload infrastructure

front:
DR: Warm standby

How does it differ from pilot light?
back: A scaled-down but fully functional copy of production is always running in another Region, so recovery is faster.

src.title: AWS Docs: Disaster recovery options in the cloud
src.q: The warm standby approach involves ensuring that there is a scaled down, but fully functional, copy of your production environment in another Region

front:
DR: Multi-site active/active

What is the trade-off?
back: Serves traffic from all Regions. Most complex and costly, but recovery time can be near zero.

src.title: AWS Docs: Disaster recovery options in the cloud
src.q: This approach is the most complex and costly approach to disaster recovery, but it can reduce your recovery time to near zero for most disasters

front:
Amazon EFS

How is it shared and sized?
back: Serverless, fully elastic file storage shared by many instances, with no provisioning of capacity.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Amazon EFS?
src.q: Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) provides serverless, fully elastic file storage

front:
EBS performance

What else affects volume performance?
back: Instance configuration, I/O characteristics and workload demand, not only volume type. Use EBS-optimized instances to use provisioned IOPS fully.

src.title: AWS Docs: EBS volume types
src.q: There are several factors that can affect the performance of EBS volumes

front:
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server

When do you pick it?
back: To lift and shift Windows applications needing fully managed Windows file servers with a native Windows file system.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is FSx for Windows?
src.q: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers, backed by a fully native Windows file system

front:
S3 Transfer Acceleration

What does it speed up?
back: Long-distance transfers between a client and an S3 bucket, using CloudFront's globally distributed edge locations.

src.title: AWS Docs: S3 Transfer Acceleration
src.q: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration is a bucket-level feature that enables fast, easy, and secure transfers of files over long distances

front:
Cluster placement group

What is it good for?
back: Low-latency, tightly coupled node-to-node communication, like HPC. Packs instances close together inside one AZ.

src.title: AWS Docs: Placement groups
src.q: Packs instances close together inside an Availability Zone

front:
Partition placement group

What does it isolate?
back: Groups of instances in one partition do not share underlying hardware with other partitions. Good for large distributed systems.

src.title: AWS Docs: Placement groups
src.q: Spreads your instances across logical partitions so that groups of instances in one partition do not share the underlying hardware

front:
Amazon ElastiCache

What does it provide?
back: A distributed in-memory data store or cache to reduce database load and give low-latency reads.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is ElastiCache?
src.q: Amazon ElastiCache is a web service that makes it easy to set up, manage, and scale a distributed in-memory data store or cache environment in the cloud

front:
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)

What response time does it target?
back: Microseconds, for eventually consistent reads, as an in-memory cache in front of DynamoDB.

src.title: AWS Docs: DynamoDB Accelerator
src.q: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) delivers fast response times for accessing eventually consistent data

front:
DynamoDB capacity modes

Name the two.
back: On-demand and provisioned. The mode also decides how you are charged for reads and writes.

src.title: AWS Docs: DynamoDB read/write capacity mode
src.q: you can choose between on-demand mode and provisioned mode for your tables

front:
Amazon CloudFront

What does it deliver?
back: Static and dynamic web content to users faster, from a global network of edge locations.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is CloudFront?
src.q: Amazon CloudFront is a web service that speeds up distribution of your static and dynamic web content

front:
AWS Global Accelerator

What does it improve?
back: Application performance for local and global users through accelerators, using static anycast IPs and the AWS network.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Global Accelerator?
src.q: AWS Global Accelerator is a service in which you create accelerators to improve the performance of your applications for local and global users

front:
VPC peering

How do VPCs communicate?
back: Privately, as if on the same network, without traversing the internet. No gateway needed, and no single point of failure.

src.title: AWS Docs: VPC peering
src.q: This private connection allows resources in the peered VPCs to interact with each other as if they were part of the same network

front:
AWS Transit Gateway

When is it better than many peering links?
back: As a hub interconnecting many VPCs and on-premises networks, instead of a mesh of point-to-point peerings.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Transit Gateway?
src.q: AWS Transit Gateway is a network transit hub used to interconnect virtual private clouds (VPCs) and on-premises networks

front:
Kinesis Data Streams

What does it handle?
back: Collecting and processing large streams of data records in real time.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Kinesis Data Streams?
src.q: You can use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to collect and process large streams of data records in real time

front:
Amazon Athena

What do you query, and with what?
back: Data directly in S3 using standard SQL, serverless with no infrastructure to manage.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Athena?
src.q: Amazon Athena is an interactive query service that makes it easy to analyze data directly in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) using standard SQL

front:
AWS Glue

What does it do?
back: Serverless data integration: discover, prepare, move and combine data from multiple sources (ETL).

src.title: AWS Docs: What is AWS Glue?
src.q: AWS Glue is a serverless data integration service that makes it easy for analytics users to discover, prepare, move, and integrate data from multiple sources

front:
S3 storage classes

Why are there several?
back: To optimize storage costs, performance and availability for your objects. The default is S3 Standard.

src.title: AWS Docs: S3 storage classes
src.q: Choosing a storage class designed for your use case lets you optimize storage costs, performance, and availability for your objects

front:
S3 Lifecycle

What are the two action types?
back: Transition actions (move to another storage class) and expiration actions (delete). A set of rules applied to groups of objects.

src.title: AWS Docs: Managing object lifecycle
src.q: An S3 Lifecycle configuration is a set of rules that define actions that Amazon S3 applies to a group of objects

front:
S3 Intelligent-Tiering

When is it a good choice?
back: When access patterns are unknown or change. It moves objects between access tiers automatically to save cost.

src.title: AWS Docs: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
src.q: S3 Intelligent-Tiering delivers automatic cost savings by moving data on a granular object level between access tiers when access patterns change

front:
Savings Plans

What do you commit to?
back: A consistent amount of compute usage (USD per hour) for 1 or 3 years, in return for lower prices than On-Demand. More flexible than Reserved Instances.

src.title: AWS Docs: What are Savings Plans?
src.q: Savings Plans provide savings beyond On-Demand rates in exchange for a commitment of using a specified amount of compute power

front:
Reserved Instances

How do they differ from Savings Plans?
back: You commit to a specific instance configuration, while Savings Plans commit to a usage amount and allow different configurations.

src.title: AWS Docs: Reserved Instances
src.q: With Reserved Instances, you make a commitment to a specific instance configuration

front:
Spot Instances

What workloads suit them?
back: Flexible, interruptible work: batch, stateless, fault-tolerant. Deep discounts for unused capacity that can be reclaimed.

src.title: AWS Docs: Spot Instances
src.q: Spot Instances are a cost-effective choice if you can be flexible about when your applications run and if your applications can be interrupted

front:
AWS Compute Optimizer

What does it recommend?
back: Rightsizing recommendations and idle resources, based on configuration and utilization metrics.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Compute Optimizer?
src.q: to provide you with rightsizing recommendations and identify idle resources

front:
DynamoDB on-demand vs provisioned

Which fits unpredictable traffic?
back: On-demand (pay per request, no capacity planning). Provisioned suits predictable traffic and can be cheaper.

src.title: AWS Docs: DynamoDB read/write capacity mode
src.q: you can choose between on-demand mode and provisioned mode for your tables

front:
AWS Budgets

What can it track and trigger?
back: Costs, usage, and RI or Savings Plans coverage and utilization, with alerts and actions when thresholds are crossed.

src.title: AWS Docs: Managing costs with AWS Budgets
src.q: You can use AWS Budgets to track and take action on your AWS costs and usage

front:
AWS Cost Explorer

What do you analyze with it?
back: Your usage and costs over time, using graphs and reports, to find drivers and trends.

src.title: AWS Docs: What is Cost Explorer?
src.q: You can explore your usage and costs using the main graph, the Cost Explorer cost and usage reports, or the Cost Explorer RI reports
